sourceNote: Reviewed all supplied events E0–E1510. The transcript contains transcription errors and events crossing speaker boundaries; U marks those mixed events. Attribution follows conversational context rather than approximate anchors: notably, E793–E798 continues O'Connor's challenge. No audio or external sources were consulted. Findings concern claim use, not historical accuracy or debate performance.

teaserSpans.reason: Opening montage replays excerpts appearing later at E133–E135, E816–E819, and E581–E586.
Inserted archival debate excerpt and applause within the introduction; this is editorial footage rather than the present conversation. Its wording is not replayed later in the supplied transcript.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: he will be willing to hold to it even in the face of evidence to the contrary
candidates.explanation: Personal acquaintance with God is offered as a reason to retain belief despite contrary evidence, with hoped-for answers at E612–E615. Whether this grants unrestricted immunity remains unclear: the misinformation example supplies an argument, and E618–E626 explicitly rejects believing against actual facts. This is a qualified epistemic argument, not a compact slogan.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: we're never going to have evidence that the actual bones of Jesus were were found
candidates.explanation: Craig concedes that actual discovery would falsify resurrection at E660–E663, then rules out ever evidentially identifying such a discovery and preserves an always-available tomb denial at E670–E672. Archaeological uncertainty supplies an ordinary reason, but its unrestricted application protects against this proposed test. The protection is specific to this test, not demonstrably every objection.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.explanation: The maxim supports asking for stronger resurrection evidence, but its secular evidential requirement is not explained here. O'Connor presents it for assessment rather than as an unquestionable rule, supplies a separate divine-intention argument at E804–E815, and later discusses prior probabilities at E914–E945. These qualifications make substitution uncertain; no criticism-blocking device appears.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: people don't die for a lie that they have themselves made up
candidates.explanation: The categorical maxim bridges willingness to die and sincerity without establishing that knowing fabricators cannot accept death or lack an escape. O'Connor identifies the recantation gap at E1083–E1091; Craig acknowledges uncertainty at E1092–E1093. His independent cultural argument and later emphasis on suffering support plausibility, but do not establish the maxim's categorical exclusion.

contrasts.speaker: A
contrasts.quote: you can have ordinary evidence that will be sufficient to establish an extraordinary event
contrasts.explanation: Craig explains the claim through the relative likelihood of evidence under competing hypotheses. Whatever the dispute over 'extraordinary,' the compact conclusion accompanies an explicit probabilistic reason rather than replacing one.

contrasts.speaker: B
contrasts.quote: people do die for things that they mistakenly think are true but are in fact false
contrasts.explanation: O'Connor provisionally accepts the sincerity inference and identifies its limit: sincere belief does not establish truth. He then proposes hallucination as an alternative to investigate. The distinction does explicit inferential work without asserting that the alternative is proven.
